reason: The passage portrays the established religious and political elite unfavorably in stark contrast to the young Samuel. Eli, the high priest, is depicted as physically weak (blind eyes that 'could not see'), failing to restrain his wicked sons, and ultimately dying in shame when receiving news of military disaster and the capture of the Ark. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are explicitly portrayed as causing people to curse them due to their wickedness. The elders of Israel, in their collective wisdom, make a strategic error by believing the Ark itself will save them, leading to the deaths of 30,000 men and the loss of the Ark to the Philistines. Samuel, by contrast, is a young servant (not part of the established elite) who is portrayed extremely favorably—obedient, faithful, chosen by God, and eventually established as a reliable prophet throughout Israel. The passage creates a moral contrast: the corrupt or ineffective elite fail and suffer judgment, while the humble outsider becomes the instrument of God's will.
